data.title: Trzcinica – the Carpathian Troy and the oldest ramparts of Lesser Poland
data.excerpt: Trzcinica near Jasło, known as the Carpathian Troy, is the best-preserved early medieval hillfort in Lesser Poland and one of the oldest Slavic hillforts of all: its ramparts still stand 10 m high and take up 3.5 ha. Excavations here have revealed the oldest defended settlements known in Poland until then, together with the first direct confirmation of links with the Anatolian–Balkan culture.

children.text: On an eminence above the valley of the little river Ropa, about 5 km from the town of Jasło in the Carpathian region of Poland, people have long known a place with high banks which they called the “Royal Ramparts” (figs 1, 2).

As early as the beginning of the 19th century 3 pagan sanctuaries were uncovered here and lovers of antiquities began to take an interest in the place. The first professional excavation took place as early as 1957, and a detailed archaeological …in the years 1991–1996 and 2005–2009, and it brought sensational discoveries (fig. 3). The oldest defended settlements known until then were discovered, as well as the first direct confirmation of the civilisational interactions of the territory of Poland with the Anatolian–Balkan culture.

Trzcinica is the best-preserved early medieval hillfort in Lesser Poland and one of the oldest Slavic hillforts of all. The defensive ramparts, measured from the base of the banks, still reach a height of 10 m today and take up 3.5 ha of ground.
 Initially a guard hillfort with an entrance from the side of the ravine was built here. The settlement was protected by a rampart with a timber-and-earth palisade (fig. 4), by ditches and by …with a gradient of 20–40° and 30 m high. It was inhabited by the people of the “Pleszów phase of the Mierzanowice culture” (2100–1650 BC; traces of occupation by this culture have also been found in the surroundings of Bardejov) with strong sub-Carpathian elements. Characteristic of it was clay tableware decorated with cord impressions, grooves, small knobs, applied strips and ribbing. The inhabitants were engaged in farming, animal husbandry, hunting, fishing, weaving and the working of stone tools.

In the years 1650–1350 BC a community of the advanced Otomani-Füzesabony culture lived here. It built a new road into the hillfort, rebuilt and strengthened the fortifications and, after they burned down, rebuilt the fortification and enlarged the settlement to an area of 2 ha by adding a bailey, securing it with palisades and ditches on the side of the easiest approach (fig. 6). It established trade contacts towards the sea to the south and to the north, and there was a development in the metallurgy of bronze and gold. Besides the aristocratic layer, the population was more numerously represented above all by warriors and serfs (that is, slaves). Their main occupations were the cultivation of the land, the raising of domestic animals, fishing and long-distance trade. The graves were richly furnished. The people of the Otomani-Füzesabony culture inhabited above all the north-eastern part of the Carpathian Basin.

In the period of the Early Middle Ages (AD 780–1031) there was an enormous seat here, the central hillfort of one of the Slavic tribes inhabiting Lesser Poland at that time. Its construction cost enormous effort and toil and no little artistry and skill (fig. 7).

The hillfort measured 115 × 275 m and consisted of an acropolis (the central hillfort) and three baileys. The ramparts were set from the north at intervals of between 60 and 70 m; the rampart protecting bailey I was about 5 m high, while bailey II was protected by a rampart more than 9 m high with a base 22–24 m wide. The rampart of bailey III was the lowest, reaching a height of only 2 m, and it supplemented the defence of the preceding ramparts from the north, while the ramparts of baileys I and II encircled the hillfort and also protected the acropolis itself from the south (fig. 15). The timber-and-earth ramparts were constructed as grillage, palisade and wattle structures and were more than 1,250 m long. The grillage ramparts were 3.5–5 m wide, the wattle ones 3.5 m and the palisade ones 2.2 m. For their construction 25,000 m³ of building material was used, of which about 6,000 m³ was timber, mostly oak. The hillfort was surrounded by several open settlements, where people lived in log houses and semi-sunken buildings (fig. 8). The destruction of the hillfort as a result of fire appears most probable in AD 1031, at the end of the reign of Mieszko II, or during the internal unrest in Poland in the years 1034–1039.

In the 20th and 21st centuries more than 160,000 artefacts were studied in an interdisciplinary way and the defensive construction was investigated. Many kinds of clay and ceramic vessels were found, as well as objects of bone and antler, worked stones and flints, and unique objects of bronze and iron. Cult objects, prehistoric works of art, implements, weapons and ornaments were found. Unusually valuable proved to be an early medieval silver hoard consisting of coins, ornaments of various kinds, pieces of silver and a unique mount from a sword scabbard (figs 9, 10). Throughout the whole time of the functioning of the defended site at Trzcinica, varied cultural influences are attested. Inhumation graves are attested only from the 11th century.

The idea of establishing the “Carpathian Troy Open-Air Archaeological Museum” precisely here arose as early as 1998; the park covers an area of more than 8 ha (of which 3.5 ha is the hillfort) and the whole project cost more than 13 million zloty (about 3.1 million EUR), with the EU contributing 1.7 million EUR.

At the hillfort there are now reconstructed sections of the defensive ramparts (figs 11, 12) and of houses. You can find there 9 sections of the defensive ramparts (fig. 13), a section of the fortification, of the access road and of the gateway, and two houses of the Bronze Age, 4 Slavic houses, the entrance gateway (fig. 16), a spring of water from the 10th century (fig. 14) and the place where the hoard was hidden.

Apart from a few coins from Bohemia, the source says nothing about the influence of Great Moravia, even though this territory lay within the sphere of influence (of tribute) of Great Moravia under the ruler Samo and under the Great Moravian rulers. (translator's note)
